Chapter 1: What is RAG?

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, is an architectural pattern that enhances large language models (LLMs) by connecting them to external knowledge sources. Instead of relying solely on what the model learned during training, RAG lets the model look up relevant information before generating a response.

Think of it like giving a student an open-book exam. Without RAG, the student must answer from memory alone (closed-book). With RAG, the student can search through reference materials and then compose an answer using both the retrieved facts and their own reasoning ability.
Why RAG Matters
LLMs have a fixed knowledge cutoff — they don't know about recent events
LLMs can hallucinate — they make up plausible-sounding but incorrect information
LLMs cannot access proprietary or private data by default
RAG is cost-effective — no need to retrain or fine-tune the model
RAG provides attribution — you can cite the source documents used
RAG is updatable — swap in new data without touching the model
RAG combines the best of two worlds: retrieval (searching for factual information) and generation (composing coherent responses). The retrieval grounds the generation in reality.
The Core Idea
A RAG system has three main components that work together in sequence:
Ingest — Documents are processed, split into chunks, converted to embeddings, and stored in a vector database
Retrieve — When a user asks a question, it is converted to the same embedding space, and the system searches for the most relevant document chunks
Generate — The retrieved chunks are injected into the LLM's prompt as context, and the LLM generates a grounded response

Chapter 2: The Problem RAG Solves

Before understanding why RAG is revolutionary, we must understand the fundamental limitations of large language models. LLMs are remarkable, but they have three critical weaknesses that RAG directly addresses.
The Knowledge Cutoff Problem

Every LLM is trained on a snapshot of data collected up to a specific date. For example, GPT-4's training data cuts off in April 2023. If you ask it about an event from last week, it literally cannot know the answer — it was never trained on that information.
Think of it like a encyclopedia published in 2020. It's excellent for historical facts, but useless for current events. RAG solves this by giving the model access to up-to-date external data.
The Hallucination Problem

LLMs are designed to generate plausible-sounding text, not to be factually correct. When they don't know an answer, they often confabulate — they make something up that sounds convincing. This is called hallucination.
In high-stakes domains like medicine, law, or finance, hallucinations are unacceptable. RAG mitigates this by providing factual context that constrains the model's output.
The Data Isolation Problem

Organizations have vast amounts of private data — internal documentation, customer records, proprietary research — that no public LLM can access. Fine-tuning on this data is expensive, slow, and requires ML expertise.
RAG provides a practical alternative: keep your data in a vector database, retrieve what's relevant at query time, and never expose the underlying data to the model during training.

text: When NOT to Use RAG
When you need real-time responses with zero added latency
When your queries never require external or up-to-date knowledge
When you have highly structured data better served by traditional databases
When the retrieval step itself is too costly for your use case

Engineering Insight: RAG introduces a latency trade-off. Each retrieval adds 100-500ms, but the quality improvement is often dramatic. In practice, the retrieval latency is usually unnoticeable to end users.
Key Takeaways
RAG addresses three fundamental LLM weaknesses: knowledge cutoff, hallucinations, and data isolation
RAG is the most practical way to give LLMs access to private or real-time data
RAG adds some latency but dramatically improves factual accuracy
Chapter 3: Embeddings — The Foundation
Embeddings are the mathematical backbone of every RAG system. To understand RAG, you must first understand what an embedding is and how it captures meaning.
What is an Embedding?

An embedding is a dense vector (a list of numbers) that represents the semantic meaning of a piece of text. Unlike traditional keyword-based approaches, embeddings capture meaning, context, and relationships between words and concepts.

Think of it like GPS coordinates for meaning. Just as (40.7128, -74.0060) uniquely identifies New York City, an embedding vector like [0.23, -0.45, 0.89, ...] uniquely identifies the meaning of a sentence. Similar sentences have similar coordinates.
How Embeddings Capture Meaning

Modern embedding models (like text-embedding-3-small or all-MiniLM-L6-v2) are trained on massive text corpora. During training, the model learns to position semantically similar texts close together in vector space and dissimilar texts far apart.

The key insight: distance in vector space = difference in meaning. Two sentences about cats will have vectors that are close together (small distance), while a sentence about cats and one about quantum physics will be far apart (large distance).
Visualizing Vector Space
While real embeddings have 384 to 3072 dimensions, we can visualize the concept in 2D. Clusters of related concepts form naturally:

In this simplified 2D projection of an embedding space, notice how "dog", "puppy", and "canine" cluster together near the bottom-left, while "car", "truck", and "vehicle" form their own cluster upper-right. The distance between clusters reflects semantic difference.
Common Embedding Models
Important: The input text and the query must use the same embedding model to produce compatible vectors. Always use the same embedding model for indexing and retrieval.
Key Takeaways
Embeddings are numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning
Similar meanings = similar vectors (close together in vector space)
Embedding dimension ranges from 384 to 3072 depending on the model
The same embedding model must be used for both indexing and retrieval
Open-source models (MiniLM, BGE, E5) make local RAG systems practical
Chapter 4: Chunking Strategies

Before documents can be searched, they must be split into manageable pieces called chunks. Chunking seems simple — just split text — but the strategy you choose dramatically impacts retrieval quality.
Why Chunking Matters

Think of chunking as deciding the granularity of your knowledge base. Too large, and each chunk contains multiple topics — the embedding becomes muddled. Too small, and individual chunks lack sufficient context to be useful.
The goal is to create chunks that are semantically self-contained — each chunk should express one complete idea or piece of information.
Chunking Approaches Compared

rows: Split every N characters/tokens with optional overlap
Use embeddings to detect topic boundaries

text: The Overlap Trick
A simple but effective technique: when chunking, overlap consecutive chunks by 10-20%. This ensures that information near chunk boundaries isn't lost:
Chunk 1: [The cat sat on the mat. The mat was]
Chunk 2: [The mat was old and worn. The cat purred.]
The overlapping phrase "The mat was" ensures both chunks carry context across the boundary.
Chunk Size Trade-offs

caption: The trade-off between chunk size, precision, and context richness

text: Practical Guidelines
Start with 512 tokens — this is a well-balanced default for most use cases
Use 10-20% overlap to avoid information loss at boundaries
Chunk at semantic boundaries (paragraphs, sections) not arbitrary token counts
For Q&A, aim for chunks that each contain one question-answerable fact
Test different chunk sizes — there is no universally correct value

Production Tip: Use LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter as your starting point. It splits on natural delimiters (double newline → single newline → sentence end) and automatically handles overlap.
Key Takeaways
Chunking determines the granularity of your knowledge base
512 tokens with 20% overlap is a strong default
Chunk at natural semantic boundaries, not arbitrary positions
Overlap prevents information loss at chunk boundaries
Different document types may need different chunking strategies
Chapter 5: Vector Databases
Once you have converted documents into embedding vectors, you need a place to store them — and more importantly, a way to search them by similarity. This is what vector databases do.
What Makes Vector Databases Special?

Traditional databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) are optimized for exact matches — they find rows where a column equals a specific value. Vector databases are optimized for similarity search — they find vectors closest to a given query vector.

Think of it like the difference between a library catalog (traditional DB) and a friend who knows your taste (vector DB). The catalog tells you exactly where a specific book is. Your friend says, "Based on what you liked before, you'll probably enjoy these."
Popular Vector Databases Compared
How Vector Search Works
Behind the scenes, vector databases use specialized index structures to enable fast similarity search. The most common approach is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World):
Vectors are stored in a graph structure organized by layers
The top layer has few nodes (long-range connections)
Lower layers have more nodes (fine-grained connections)
Search starts at the top layer and descends — like taking a highway then local roads
This achieves O(log n) search complexity — millions of vectors searched in milliseconds
Distance Metrics
Important: Most modern embedding models produce normalized vectors. For normalized vectors, cosine similarity and dot product produce the same ranking. Check your embedding model's documentation.
Key Takeaways
Vector databases enable similarity search over embeddings
HNSW is the most widely used indexing algorithm for vector search
ChromaDB and FAISS are excellent choices for getting started locally
Distance metrics matter — cosine similarity is the default for semantic search
For production, consider managed services (Pinecone) or full-featured engines (Weaviate, Qdrant)
Chapter 6: Retrieval & Semantic Search
Retrieval is the heart of any RAG system. It determines which pieces of information the LLM will see. A good retrieval system finds the right context; a bad one feeds irrelevant noise.
Semantic Search vs. Keyword Search

Traditional keyword search (like grep or SQL LIKE) looks for exact word matches. If you search for "canine", you won't find documents mentioning "dog". Semantic search understands meaning — it finds "dog" documents even when you search for "canine".
Think of keyword search as a jigsaw puzzle — you need the exact piece. Semantic search is like a magnet — it pulls in all nearby pieces regardless of their shape.
ANN Search: Speed vs. Accuracy

Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search is the technique behind all modern vector databases. Instead of measuring distance to every single vector (which would be O(n) and prohibitively slow for millions of vectors), ANN uses smart indexing to find approximate neighbors in O(log n) time.
The trade-off: ANN is approximate, not exact. You might miss the true nearest neighbor, but you'll find one that's close enough — and you'll do it 100-1000x faster.
Retrieval Quality Metrics

rows: Of top-K results, how many are relevant?
Of all relevant documents, how many are in top-K?
Mean Reciprocal Rank — how early is the first relevant result?
Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain — ranking quality

text: Hybrid Search: Best of Both Worlds

Hybrid search combines semantic search (embedding similarity) with keyword search (BM25) and fuses the results. This catches cases where exact keyword matches matter (like product codes or names) while still benefiting from semantic understanding.
The fusion is typically done with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which combines rankings from multiple sources:
RRF score = 1/(60 + rank_semantic) + 1/(60 + rank_keyword)
The Retrieval Flow

caption: Hybrid retrieval pipeline combining semantic and keyword search with RRF fusion

text: Production Tip: A reranker step (also called a cross-encoder) re-scores the top 20-50 results with a more accurate model. This dramatically improves precision at the cost of a small latency increase. Use models like BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3.
Key Takeaways
Semantic search finds by meaning, keyword search finds by exact match
ANN makes vector search practical at scale (O(log n) vs. O(n))
Hybrid search (semantic + BM25 + RRF) is more robust than either alone
A reranker step before the LLM significantly improves final quality
Measure retrieval quality with Precision@K and Recall@K

The Augmented Prompt
The key innovation in RAG is how retrieved context is injected into the prompt. A typical augmented prompt looks like this:

SYSTEM: You are a helpful assistant. Use the following context
to answer the user's question. If you cannot find the answer
in the context, say so — do not make up information.

CONTEXT:
---
[Document 1]: The Python garbage collector uses reference
counting and a cycle detector.
---
[Document 2]: Memory management in Python is automatic.
Objects are deallocated when their reference count reaches zero.
---
[Document 3]: The gc module provides control over the
cyclic garbage collector.
---

USER: How does Python handle memory management?

ASSISTANT:

Important: Always instruct the LLM to refuse answering if the context doesn't contain relevant information. This prevents the model from falling back on its training data and potentially hallucinating.
Key Takeaways
RAG has two phases: Indexing (offline) and Query (online)
The indexing pipeline: Load → Split → Embed → Store
The query pipeline: Embed query → Search → Retrieve → Augment prompt → Generate
The augmented prompt contains retrieved context + the original question
Always instruct the LLM to only answer from the provided context
Chapter 8: Building a RAG System in Python
In this chapter, we'll build a complete RAG system step by step using Python. We'll use LangChain for orchestration, ChromaDB for the vector store, and open-source embedding models.
Setup & Installation

pip install langchain langchain-community langchain-chroma
pip install chromadb sentence-transformers pypdf
Step 1: Load a PDF Document

from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader

loader = PyPDFLoader("handbook.pdf")
documents = loader.load()
print(f"Loaded {len(documents)} pages")
Step 2: Split into Chunks

from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=512,
    chunk_overlap=64,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ".", "!", "?"],
    length_function=len,
)

chunks = splitter.split_documents(documents)
print(f"Created {len(chunks)} chunks")
Step 3: Create Embeddings & Vector Store

from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings

embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    model_kwargs={"device": "cpu"},
    encode_kwargs={"normalize_embeddings": True},
)

vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(
    documents=chunks,
    embedding=embeddings,
    persist_directory="./chroma_db",
)

print(f"Stored {vectorstore._collection.count()} vectors")
Step 4: Set Up the Retriever

retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(
    search_type="similarity",
    search_kwargs={"k": 4},
)
Step 5: Create the RAG Chain
Step 6: Ask Questions!

result = rag_chain.invoke(
    "What is the company policy on remote work?"
)
print(result.content)
Full Working Example with FAISS

from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain_community.document_loaders import TextLoader
from langchain.text_splitter import CharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA

loader = TextLoader("knowledge_base.txt")
docs = loader.load()

text_splitter = CharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50
)
chunks = text_splitter.split_documents(docs)

embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embeddings)

qa = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(
    llm=ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0),
    chain_type="stuff",
    retriever=vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 3}),
    return_source_documents=True,
)

response = qa.invoke(
    {"query": "What are the main features?"}
)
print(response["result"])
print(f"Sources: {len(response['source_documents'])}")

Engineering Insight: The `return_source_documents=True` flag lets you inspect which documents the model used to generate its answer. This is crucial for debugging and building trust with users through citations.
Key Takeaways
LangChain provides clean abstractions for building RAG pipelines
ChromaDB is ideal for prototyping; FAISS offers more speed for local use
Always include a "don't know" instruction in your prompt to prevent hallucination
Return source documents for debugging and attribution
Open-source embedding models (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) work well for local development
Chapter 9: Advanced RAG Patterns
Once you master basic RAG, there are several advanced patterns that address specific limitations. Three of the most important are Agentic RAG, Graph RAG, and HyDE.
Agentic RAG: Let the LLM Drive
In basic RAG, the retriever always runs, always retrieves the same number of documents (k), and always injects them into the prompt. Agentic RAG gives the LLM agency over the retrieval process:
The LLM decides whether to retrieve — it can skip retrieval for simple queries
The LLM decides what to search for — it can reformulate or decompose queries
The LLM decides when to retrieve — it can do multiple rounds of research
The LLM can use tools — calling APIs, querying databases, or browsing the web
Think of it like a research assistant who doesn't just hand you pre-selected documents but actively decides what to look up, in what order, and whether more information is needed.
Agentic RAG Flow

caption: Agentic RAG — the LLM controls its own retrieval process

text: Graph RAG: Structured Knowledge

Graph RAG (developed by Microsoft) extracts entities and relationships from documents to build a knowledge graph. Instead of searching over raw text chunks, Graph RAG queries the graph structure, enabling:
Multi-hop reasoning: "What products does the CEO's former company make?"
Global summarization: Summarize themes across the entire knowledge base
Relationship-aware retrieval: Find documents connected through entities
Think of it as the difference between a file cabinet (basic RAG) and a mind map (Graph RAG). The file cabinet stores documents; the mind map shows how everything connects.
HyDE: Hypothetical Document Embeddings

HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) is a clever technique: instead of searching with the user's question directly, you first ask an LLM to generate a hypothetical answer, then use that answer as the search query.

The insight: queries and documents live in different regions of embedding space. A question like "What causes inflation?" is structurally different from a document about inflation. By generating a hypothetical document first, HyDE bridges this gap.
Patterns Comparison

Production Tip: Start with basic RAG and hybrid search. Only add Agentic or Graph RAG if your evaluation shows clear gaps that simpler approaches cannot fill. Complexity should be earned, not assumed.
Key Takeaways
Agentic RAG gives the LLM control over when and what to retrieve
Graph RAG extracts entities and relationships for structured reasoning
HyDE improves retrieval by searching with a hypothetical answer instead of the question
Start simple — add complexity only when evaluation proves it necessary
The RAG ecosystem is rapidly evolving; these patterns represent the current frontier
Chapter 10: Production Considerations
Building a RAG system that works on your laptop is one thing. Running it reliably in production is another. This chapter covers the critical considerations for production-ready RAG.
Performance & Latency
A production RAG system must balance speed, quality, and cost. Here are the typical latency contributions:
Evaluation: Is Your RAG System Good?
You cannot improve what you don't measure. A comprehensive RAG evaluation framework should track:
Retrieval Quality: Precision@K, Recall@K, MRR
Generation Quality: Faithfulness (does output match context?), Answer Relevance
End-to-End Quality: Human evaluation, task completion rate
Operational Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, cost per query
Tools like RAGAS (RAG Assessment) provide automated evaluation metrics. TruLens and LangSmith offer observability and tracing.
Security Considerations
Data exfiltration: Ensure retrieved documents cannot be leaked through prompt injection
Access control: Users should only retrieve documents they have permission to see
Content filtering: Screen retrieved content for PII, toxic content, or policy violations
Prompt injection: Protect against poisoned documents that manipulate the LLM
Rate limiting: Protect your vector DB and LLM API from abuse

Production Tip: Implement a "human in the loop" for high-stakes retrieval. Flag ambiguous or low-confidence retrievals for human review. This is especially critical in healthcare, legal, and financial applications.
